meta.ogDescription: Genuine Brontë, from Jane Eyre (1847), ch. VI — but it is Helen Burns talking, not the author. Traced to the first edition, vol. I, p. 103.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1816–1855 · English novelist and poet, published as Currer Bell
answer.sourceLine: Genuine Brontë prose, and traceable to the page: the sentence appears in Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, chapter VI, first published in October 1847 by Smith, Elder & Co. under the pen name Currer Bell. One caveat the quote cards never mention — it is not Brontë speaking in her own voice but her character Helen Burns, answering Jane’s complaint about Mrs. Reed.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Chapter VI — Helen Burns, replying to Jane at Lowood
19 October 1847 · Smith, Elder & Co., London · three volumes, as “Currer Bell”

source.excerpt: “She has been unkind to you, no doubt; because you see, she dislikes your cast of character, as Miss Scatcherd does mine; but how minutely you remember all she has done and said to you! What a singularly deep impression her injustice seems to have made on your heart! No ill-usage so brands its record on my feelings. Would you not be happier if you tried to forget her severity, together with the passionate emotions it excited? Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Jane Eyre (1847) section, sourced to “Helen Burns to Jane (Ch. 6)” — a speaker, not a floating aphorism.
The full text of chapter VI at Lit2Go ↗ and in the Project Gutenberg edition ↗ both carry the sentence inside Helen’s long reply about forgiveness.
The scanned first edition at the Internet Archive ↗ — title page “Jane Eyre, An Autobiography, Edited by Currer Bell… London: Smith, Elder, and Co., Cornhill, 1847” — prints it on p. 103 of volume I.
Wikipedia ↗ dates the novel’s first publication to 19 October 1847, by Smith, Elder & Co., in three volumes under the pen name Currer Bell.

author.name: Charlotte Brontë
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1816–1855 · English novelist and poet, published as Currer Bell
author.bio: Charlotte Brontë was the eldest surviving of the three Brontë sisters and the author of Jane Eyre (1847), which she published under the male pen name Currer Bell. She had been sent as a child to the Clergy Daughters’ School at Cowan Bridge, where her elder sisters Maria and Elizabeth contracted the illness that killed them — the experience she reworked as Lowood, the school where this line is spoken. She outlived all five of her siblings and died in 1855, at 38.

misattribution.heading: What the quote cards get wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fabrication — the words are Brontë’s, on a page you can go and look at. What travels badly is who is speaking, and how the sentence is cut.

items.who: Charlotte Brontë, presented as speaking for herself
items.why: Goodreads prints it credited simply to “Charlotte Bronte, Jane Eyre” ↗, with no indication that the line belongs to Helen Burns. Wikiquote, by contrast, keeps the attribution the novel actually supports: “Helen Burns to Jane (Ch. 6)” ↗.

items.who: The comma-free version now standard online
items.why: The 1847 first edition ↗ prints “nursing animosity, or registering wrongs” with a comma; the widely circulated Project Gutenberg text ↗, set from an 1897 illustrated edition, drops it. Both wordings are otherwise identical, so neither is a fake — but the comma is the original.

AZQuotes runs the sentence straight into ↗ “With this creed, revenge never worries my heart…”, as if the two were consecutive. In the novel a long passage about the corruptible body and the soul’s return sits between them. Its citation also points at a 2004 reprint rather than the 1847 edition.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is authentic Charlotte Brontë, written for Helen Burns in chapter VI of Jane Eyre and printed on page 103 of volume I of the 1847 first edition ↗.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Jane has just poured out, in her own words, “the tale of my sufferings and resentments” — the cruelty of Mrs. Reed, the blows of cousin John. She expects agreement. What she gets instead is Helen Burns, the consumptive schoolfellow who takes Miss Scatcherd’s punishments without protest, gently pointing out how minutely Jane has remembered every injury. The famous sentence is the hinge of that rebuke: not a slogan about positivity, but an argument that a ledger of wrongs is a poor use of a short life.

The irony is that Brontë was writing from a real grave. Helen Burns dies of consumption in Jane’s arms at Lowood, and Lowood was drawn from the Clergy Daughters’ School at Cowan Bridge, where Charlotte’s own sisters Maria and Elizabeth caught the disease that killed them. Elizabeth Gaskell, in her biography of the sisters, called Helen Burns “an exact transcript” of Maria Brontë ↗, who died of consumption at eleven. The counsel against nursing animosity is put in the mouth of a girl modelled on a sister the school effectively killed.
context.detailsSummary: What the sentence is actually answering
detailsBody: Jane’s position, a page earlier, is the opposite one: “When we are struck at without a reason, we should strike back again very hard.” Helen’s reply builds from the New Testament to the passage that ends, many lines later, “I live in calm, looking to the end.” Read whole, it is a theological argument about forgiveness and the afterlife, not a standalone maxim — which is why quote sites so often cut it loose from everything around it.
context.pull: It is not the author’s creed on a poster. It is a dying schoolgirl talking a furious child down.

sourcesVerified.claim: The 1847 Smith, Elder first edition of Jane Eyre (vol. I, ch. VI, p. 103) contains "Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity, or registering wrongs", with a comma; title page reads "Edited by Currer Bell... London: Smith, Elder, and Co., Cornhill. 1847."
Project Gutenberg's full text of Jane Eyre contains the sentence in Chapter VI, spoken by Helen Burns, printed without a comma after "animosity"; the ebook is free and public domain in the USA.
Wikiquote lists "Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity, or registering wrongs." under its Jane Eyre (1847) section, cited as "Helen Burns to Jane (Ch. 6)".

Jane Eyre was first published on 19 October 1847 by Smith, Elder & Co. in three volumes under the pen name Currer Bell; Elizabeth Gaskell called Helen Burns "an exact transcript" of Maria Brontë, who died of consumption at age 11; Lowood derives from the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge.

Charlotte Brontë lived 21 April 1816 – 31 March 1855, was an English novelist and poet who published as Currer Bell, and attended the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge where her sisters Maria and Elizabeth fell fatally ill.

Chapter VI of Jane Eyre contains the passage "...Would you not be happier if you tried to forget her severity... Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs...", spoken by Helen Burns.
Goodreads prints the quote without a comma and credits it only to "Charlotte Bronte, Jane Eyre", with no mention of Helen Burns as the speaker.

AZQuotes presents the sentence spliced directly onto "With this creed, revenge never worries my heart, degradation never too deeply disgusts me, injustice never crushes me too low. I live in calm, looking to the end." and cites "Charlotte Bronte (2004). 'Jane Eyre', p.26, Variocity".

The British Library states that Charlotte Brontë's experiences at Cowan Bridge inspired her portrayal of the harsh conditions at Lowood School in Jane Eyre, and gives the novel's publication year as 1847 with the original subtitle "An Autobiography".
